transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-07-06
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jorge Alvarez (Redwood SE), Sophie Nguyen (Arbor Head of Platform), Ethan Park (Arbor ML Eng), Lena Brooks (Arbor Security), Omar Khalid (Arbor CTO)

Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect):
Arbor Analytics is evaluating Redwood for a hybrid deployment: hosted for quick prod features, dedicated for consistent throughput, and potential private/VPC for regulated data. They're primarily integrating via an edge gateway/proxy and using LangChain and LamaIndex style retrieval stacks. Key concerns: rate limits/quotas, observability hooks, SSO/KMS, and benchmarked latency with kv cache and batching. Next steps are SDK samples, SOC2 docs, and a technical deep dive.

Topics:
- Integration patterns: SDK vs gateway/proxy vs sidecar
- LangChain/LlamaIndex retrieval flows and embeddings pipeline
- Rate limit behaviour and token quotas (per-route, per-team)
- Observability hooks: traces, token cost breakdown, per-model dashboards
- Security: KMS, SSO/SAML, VPC peering, audit logs

[00:00] Maya (AE): Hi everyone, thanks for making time. Quick intro — I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, and Jorge is our solutions engineer. Could we do a quick round of intros from Arbor?
[00:18] Sophie: Hey, Sophie here, Head of Platform at Arbor. We run the gateway and ingestion infra.
[00:24] Ethan: Ethan, ML eng, working on the retrieval stack and embeddings.
[00:28] Lena: Lena, security — focused on compliance and data controls.
[00:31] Omar: Omar, CTO. I'll mostly listen and chime on architecture and budget.
[00:35] Jorge (SE): Great, thanks. Goal for today — understand your integration points: are you going to call Redwood via SDK from app services, or put us behind your gateway/proxy, or a hybrid? Also discuss quotas, observability hooks, and an initial benchmark plan.

[01:02] Sophie: High-level: we have a request flow where frontends call our gateway, which routes to a microservice that does retrieval with Lang Chain. The LangChain agents call model endpoints for summarization and rerank. We currently use a mix of hosted APIs and self-hosted GPUs for heavy lifting. We're evaluating Redwood for hosted and dedicated options, and maybe private for regulated docs.

[01:27] Maya: Helpful. A couple clarifying q's — what's your peak qps for inferencing and target p95 latency?
[01:34] Sophie: Right now, average RPS is modest, about 40 rps during peak across clusters, but some inference flows are latency sensitive — we want p95 under 700 ms for short prompts. For long retrievals we can accept higher.

[01:50] Omar: And budget side — we aim to avoid massive egress and token surprises. We need predictability for monthly cost.

[02:02] Jorge: Understood. On the integration side there are a few patterns we see: 1) Direct SDK — your services call Redwood SDK/REST directly. 2) Gateway/proxy — you place an adaptor in your gateway to forward LLM calls and handle auth/rate-limiting centrally. 3) Sidecar/edge — a lightweight proxy next to app containers to optimize batching/caching. Which fits you?

[02:32] Ethan: We're leaning gateway/proxy since we centralize auth and rate limiting there. Also makes it easier to run canaries and rollout model variants. But we use LangChain inside the microservice, so the LangChain client would need to hit the proxy.

[02:45] Maya: That works. We have customers who use a transparent proxy pattern where LangChain calls are routed to a local adaptor that rewrites requests and injects keys; it can also call Redwood's SDK if you want to manage retries/batching client-side.

[03:03] Sophie: Does Redwood's SDK integrate with LangChain and LlamaIndex out of the box? We use LangChain agents and LlamaIndex for search index orchestration.

[03:12] Jorge: We have SDK wrappers and example repos for LangChain and LlamaIndex. Small note — some of the example code in our quickstart uses the term Lang Chain (two words) in docs, he'll — doc generator, but the code works fine. For LlamaIndex, we've got retrieval adapters and an embeddings pipeline example that shows how to shard embeddings and warm KV cache for rerank.

[03:34] Ethan: Nice. About the KV cache — does Redwood expose hooks to warm the cache ahead of time? We noticed p95 jumps if the KV cache cold starts during a spike.

[03:44] Jorge: Good point. We support prefix/KV cache and you can pre-warm with a cache API or via repeated synthetic requests. On Redwood Dedicated, you can reserve pools that keep KV entries hot longer; on hosted there's sensible TTLs but we can tune for high-commit customers. We'll include a benchmark config to show cold vs warm scenarios.

[04:02] Lena: From security perspective, what's the data flow and where's PII persisted? We need clarity for SOC 2 and for our DLP rules.

[04:11] Maya: By default for hosted, transient prompts are not persisted for training and are retained for X days for troubleshooting; for Dedicated and Private you can have stricter retention or no retention. We support KMS for encryption at rest and in transit, and private deployments run inside your VPC with customer-managed KMS. I'll send the SOC 2 and network diagram docs after this call.

[04:33] Lena: Good, please include details on audit logs and SSO. We use SAML for SSO and need RBAC for who can change rollout policies.

[04:42] Jorge: We support SAML SSO and granular API keys and team-based RBAC. Audit logs of model calls, rollouts, and who changed config are available via the Console or exported to your SIEM.

[04:56] Omar: Cost controls — can we set per-route quotas and soft vs hard limits? We want team A to have a budget of X tokens per month but not affect team B.

[05:06] Jorge: Yes. We support per-route and per-token quotas, and soft limits that alert and hard limits that block. For Dedicated customers you can map quotas to GPU pools and set burst policies. The Console provides token-level cost breakdown and alerts when burn rates exceed thresholds.

[05:22] Sophie: For gateway pattern, latencies through our proxy add a hop. How much overhead do you see typically for gateway + Redwood hosted calls?

[05:30] Jorge: In our benchmarks, simple HTTP proxy adds ~15-35 ms network overhead depending on region; more variance comes from model latency and batching. If you do continuous batching on Redwood's runtime, you'll see better unit cost but slightly higher p95 latency for single-token requests. We can tune batch windows for your SLOs.

[05:51] Ethan: Can we control batching from the client side? For LangChain calls which are chat-like we want low latency — maybe no batching. For bulk embeddings we want aggressive batching.

[06:00] Maya: Client-side controls via SDK let you set batching policy per call: immediate, micro-batch (20-50ms), or server-side continuous batching with target latency. We'll show examples in the SDK quickstart.

[06:12] Lena: On private deployment: is there an on-prem package for air-gapped environments? If so, what's the update cadence and who manages kernels and patches?

[06:22] Jorge: We offer a Private deployment package for VPC and on-prem. For air-gapped installs we ship an image and patches; customers can opt in for Redwood-managed updates (we push signed updates) or self-managed updates with our patch bundles. We also provide replication for model artifacts — model weights are handled by your infra in private mode.

[06:40] Sophie: A practical question — we have a LangChain agent that sometimes calls multiple models (rerank -> summarize -> generate). Does Redwood support multi-model orchestrations and fallback when a model variant is down?

[06:50] Jorge: Yes, our routing supports model variants and fallback policies. You can define policies like prefer-hosted-low-latency, otherwise fallback to a smaller quantized variant, or route to Dedicated pool on heavy load. Rollouts and canaries are supported too.

[07:05] Ethan: Observability — we need traces that correlate across gateway, LangChain service, and Redwood. Do you provide trace IDs to attach to spans?

[07:12] Maya: We expose a request-id header that you can propagate. Redwood Console accepts trace spans and can ingest OpenTelemetry logs if you want deeper correlation. We also emit token-level cost metrics and per-request latency breakdown which can be exported.

[07:28] Sophie: How granular are those cost metrics? We need per-route and per-user breakdown for chargeback.

[07:35] Jorge: Per-route, per-team, and per-api-key breakdowns are available. We also provide per-model token counts and can map those to internal tenants. That data is accessible via Console and an API for billing exports.

[07:48] Lena: One more sec on encryption. For hosted, do you hold KMS keys or do you support customer-supplied keys?

[07:55] Maya: Hosted supports customer-managed keys via cloud KMS integrations; for ultimate control, Private deployment with your KMS is recommended. We'll include a doc mapping key options.

[08:06] Omar: If we start hosted for quick ship but later migrate sensitive flows to Private, what is the migration story for pinned model versions and prompts?

[08:14] Jorge: The API and configuration are consistent across hosted/dedicated/private. You can pin model versions and export configs. Migration requires moving model artifacts for Private — we provide tooling to export campaign configs, prompt templates, and pin lists. For embeddings/data, you'll need to move indices or reindex depending on your storage.

[08:34] Sophie: Back to gateway specifics — we have rate-limiting at the gateway layer today. If we want Redwood to also enforce quotas, is double enforcement tricky?

[08:42] Jorge: You can centralize enforcement one place. A common pattern: the gateway enforces coarse per-customer rate limits, Redwood enforces token quotas and model-level limits. We can support response headers indicating remaining quota so the gateway can make decisions.

[08:58] Ethan: For LangChain and LlamaIndex, do you provide an adapter or should we implement request translation?

[09:06] Jorge: We have adapters for LangChain that implement Redwood client as a drop-in. LlamaIndex adapters are examples — sometimes naming may be off in the docs (we had a generator call it LamaIndex), but the repo works. We'll share the sample repo.

[09:21] Sophie: Are there any SDK languages besides Python? Our infra has Go microservices.

[09:27] Maya: Python and Node are first-class; Go and Java SDKs are available with parity on core features though some advanced console APIs are newer. For gateway patterns, the REST API is straightforward from any language.

[09:42] Lena: For auditability, can we stream logs to our SIEM? We want every inference event including token counts and user-id mapped.

[09:50] Jorge: Yes, logs can be exported via secure forwarders to S3, Kafka, or a SIEM endpoint. We can include token counts, model id, request-id, and any custom metadata you pass.

[10:05] Omar: Performance question — you mentioned continuous batching. If we set aggressive batching to save costs, what's the tail latency impact for conversational flows?

[10:15] Jorge: It depends on batch window and request shape. Typical micro-batching (20-50 ms) adds negligible tail. Continuous batching introduces a tradeoff: you might see higher p95 for single-user interactive flows but much lower cost per token. For conversation tokens where p95 < 700ms is crucial, set micro-batch/instant. For embeddings, set larger batching.

[10:37] Sophie: Ok. Let's talk about a pilot. What's minimal footprint to get a meaningful pilot going?

[10:43] Maya: For a LangChain-driven pilot we usually do: 1) LangChain adapter integration sample in your staging, 2) Dedicated pool or hosted account with a 2-week performance benchmark, 3) shared benchmark script to run typical rerank/summarize/generate flows with KV cache cold/warm states. Jorge will prepare the script.

[11:02] Ethan: Can we control tokenization settings and truncation to manage cost? We have proprietary tokenizers in some pipelines.

[11:10] Jorge: You can pass tokenization hints; Redwood supports model-agnostic token counting in the Console and via SDK. For proprietary tokenizers, you can pre-tokenize on your side and send chunked requests; cost still measured in token units. We'll advise on best-practice for truncation.

[11:27] Lena: A compliance question — do you have data residency options in EU/US regions? We operate in EU primarily.

[11:33] Maya: Yes, we have regional hosting. For Hosted we offer EU region endpoints; Dedicated can be provisioned in particular regions; Private obviously runs wherever you deploy. We'll add region-specific notes in the follow-up doc.

[11:49] Omar: Any pitfalls you see from other customers doing gateway + LangChain?

[11:54] Jorge: A few common gotchas: 1) Not propagating request-id across layers, which makes debugging hard. 2) Double rate limiting without coordinating thresholds. 3) Cold KV cache on new deployments — warm it. 4) Surprise token growth from logs or verbose system prompts. We include checklists to avoid these.

[12:18] Sophie: Great. Can you show a quick example of how a LangChain call looks with Redwood's SDK?

[12:24] Jorge: Sure — high level: you configure Redwood client with api_key and region, instantiate the LangChain LLM wrapper, and then pass a retriever that points to your LlamaIndex. In the sample we also show how to set batching policy and add a request-id header for tracing. I'll paste the gist in the follow-up.

[12:45] Ethan: On the embeddings pipeline: do you provide dedupe or similarity thresholds as part of managed services?

[12:53] Jorge: Not as a blackbox, but we provide metrics and examples to implement dedupe client-side. For large-index embeddings we recommend sharding and incremental reindexing; we can also recommend quantization for vector storage to reduce cost.

[13:09] Lena: For the pilot, we'll need the SOC2 and a network diagram first.

[13:14] Maya: We'll email SOC2, an architecture FAQ, and a VPC peering guide by tomorrow.

[13:19] Sophie: Budget gating — if the pilot shows 10-15% cost improvement over current infra with similar latency, we can consider Dedicated; otherwise we'll stay with hybrid.

[13:28] Omar: Any early blockers? Anything we need to provision?

[13:31] Jorge: For the pilot, lane items: a staging API key, a small Dedicated pool or hosted trial account, and access to your gateway dev environment to deploy the proxy adapter. Also a sample workload (langchain prompts + embeddings) to run benchmarks.

[13:46] Ethan: We'll also want to test model failover scenarios — e.g., if the preferred model is rate-limited, can Redwood route to a cheaper quantized variant without broken outputs?

[13:57] Jorge: Yes, policy-based routing handles that; we can show examples. Note output differences when switching quantized models can affect rerank thresholds, so we'll advise on regression checks.

[14:12] Maya: Recap and next steps: 1) Maya to send SDK quickstart and LangChain/LlamaIndex repo; 2) Jorge to prepare benchmark script that covers cold/warm KV, batching policies, and multi-model flows; 3) Redwood will share SOC2, KMS options, and region availability; 4) Schedule deep technical session with Arbor infra (we suggested week of 7/12).

[14:36] Sophie: Sounds good. One more minor item — how do you surface token attribution to an end-user for chargebacks?

[14:42] Jorge: We can attach metadata to requests (user-id, team-id) and the Console export will include attributed token counts per metadata key. Many customers ingest that to their billing system.

[14:55] Lena: For legal — we'll need a data processing addendum before any PII hits hosted.

[14:59] Maya: Understood — we'll include the DPA template in the follow-up.

[15:05] Omar: If we want to pilot with hosted first and then move to Dedicated for high-volume routes, how long to provision Dedicated pools?

[15:12] Maya: Dedicated provisioning timeline is usually 2–4 weeks depending on capacity and region. We'll give an estimated timeline in the follow-up.

[15:20] Sophie: Ok that's fine. Anything else?

[15:23] Ethan: One last quick question — do you have any references of similar companies who used gateway + LangChain and migrated to Dedicated?

[15:30] Maya: We can share anonymized case studies. There's a fintech customer who used our gateway adapter with LangChain and later reserved Dedicated pools for peak trading hours. We'll include a short case study link.

[15:41] Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule.
[15:45] Omar: Thank you.

[16:00] End of recording.

Note: Transcript contains occasional audio-to-text errors (product names like LlamaIndex sometimes transcribed as "LamaIndex", "LangChain" as "Lang Chain", "KV cache" as "KV cash" in a few spots) and some overlapping crosstalk.
